meta.book_title: metricsAI: An Introduction to Econometrics with Python and AI in the Cloud

practice.concept: Descriptive analysis vs. statistical inference (Section 1.1, Key Concept 1.1)
practice.stem: Which of the following is an example of statistical inference?

options.text: Estimating the national average wage from a survey of 1,000 workers.
options.feedback: Correct. The analysis uses a sample to draw a conclusion about a broader population, which is the definition of statistical inference.

options.text: Drawing a histogram of the house sizes in the sample.
options.feedback: A histogram is a descriptive tool: it summarizes the sample you have rather than drawing conclusions about a larger population.

options.text: Computing the median price of the 29 houses in the dataset.
options.feedback: This summarizes the 29 houses you already have. Ask whether the analysis reaches beyond the data in hand.

options.text: Reporting the smallest and largest house sizes in the sample.
options.feedback: The minimum and maximum describe the sample in hand. Nothing is being concluded about houses outside the data.

practice.explanation: Key Concept 1.1: statistical inference uses sample data to draw conclusions about a broader population, while descriptive analysis summarizes the data you have (medians, histograms, ranges). Estimating the national average wage from 1,000 surveyed workers is inference.

practice.concept: Observational vs. experimental data (Section 1.4, Key Concept 1.2)
practice.stem: A researcher wants to know whether a job-training program raises earnings. Which design produces experimental data?

options.text: Randomly assigning some applicants to the program and others not, then comparing their earnings.
options.feedback: Correct. The researcher controls who gets the training, and random assignment makes the two groups comparable on average.

options.text: Comparing the earnings of people who chose to enroll with those of people who chose not to.
options.feedback: Here people selected themselves into the program. Because no one controlled who enrolled, these are observational data, and the two groups may differ in motivation or skills.

options.text: Downloading national statistics on average earnings over the last 20 years.
options.feedback: Official statistics record what happened without any controlled assignment, so they are observational data.

options.text: Surveying workers about whether they think the training helped them.
options.feedback: Opinions collected in a survey are still observational: nothing about who received the training was controlled.

practice.explanation: Key Concept 1.2: experimental data come from settings where the researcher controls the conditions, ideally by random assignment. Most economic data are observational, collected without such control.

practice.concept: Observational vs. experimental data (Section 1.4, Key Concept 1.2)
practice.stem: Because most economic data are observational, establishing causal effects usually requires more careful methods than it does with experimental data.

options.text: True
options.feedback: Correct. Without control over conditions, other factors may move together with X, so careful methods are needed to isolate causal effects.

options.text: False
options.feedback: Consider what is missing in observational data: no one controlled who received which conditions. What does that imply for separating cause from coincidence?

practice.explanation: Key Concept 1.2 and the Key Takeaways: economics relies mainly on observational data, which makes causal inference more challenging than with experimental data.

practice.concept: Types of variables: continuous, discrete, categorical (Key Takeaways)
practice.stem: Which of the following are categorical variables? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Annual household income
options.feedback: Income is measured in money and can take essentially any value in a range, so it is treated as continuous numerical.

options.text: Employment status (employed, unemployed, not in the labor force)
options.feedback: Correct: each person falls into one of several labeled groups.

options.text: Number of children in a family
options.feedback: This is a count (0, 1, 2, …), which makes it discrete numerical rather than categorical.

options.text: Type of home heating (gas, electric, solar)
options.feedback: Correct: the values are labels for groups, not quantities.

practice.explanation: Categorical variables sort observations into groups (employment status, heating type). Counts such as the number of children are discrete numerical; measurements such as income are continuous numerical.

practice.concept: Data structures: cross-section, time series, panel (Key Takeaways)
practice.stem: A survey records the annual income, number of children, and employment status of 2,000 adults, all during 2023. What kind of data are these?

options.text: Time-series data
options.feedback: A time series follows one unit across many periods. Here there are many units and a single period.

options.text: Experimental data
options.feedback: The survey simply records information; nothing was assigned by the researcher. The question is about how the data are organized across units and time.

options.text: Panel data
options.feedback: Panel data follow the same units across several periods. Each adult here is observed only in 2023.

options.text: Cross-section data
options.feedback: Correct: many units (adults) observed at one point in time.

practice.explanation: Cross-section data: many units at one point in time. Time series: one unit over time. Panel: many units, each observed over time.

practice.concept: Data structures: cross-section, time series, panel (Key Takeaways)
practice.stem: A dataset that tracks the same 50 U.S. states every year from 2000 to 2020 is an example of time-series data.

options.text: True
options.feedback: Count the units: is one unit being followed over time, or many?

options.text: False
options.feedback: Correct. Many units (50 states), each observed over many years, form panel data.

practice.explanation: A time series follows a single unit over time; panel data follow many units over time (here, 50 states × 21 years).

practice.concept: Visual exploration before regression (Section 1.5, Key Concept 1.3)
practice.stem: What can a scatter plot of Y against X reveal that a summary-statistics table (count, mean, standard deviation, minimum, and maximum of each variable) cannot?

options.text: The number of observations in the dataset
options.feedback: The summary-statistics table already reports the count of observations, so you don't need a plot for that.

options.text: The average value of each variable
options.feedback: Means appear directly in the summary-statistics table; a plot is not needed to see them.

options.text: Whether X causes Y
options.feedback: No plot can establish causation on its own. It shows how the variables move together, which is association.

options.text: The form of the relationship (straight or curved) and any outliers
options.feedback: Correct. Summary statistics describe each variable separately; only a plot shows the shape of their joint pattern and any unusual points.

practice.explanation: Key Concept 1.3: scatter plots reveal the direction, strength, and form of a relationship, and expose outliers, which summary statistics alone would miss.

practice.concept: Visual exploration before regression (Section 1.5, Key Concept 1.3)
practice.stem: A scatter plot of daily ice-cream sales (Y) against daily temperature (X) shows sales rising steadily up to about 30°C and then flattening out. What should you conclude before fitting a straight line?

options.text: The plot proves that higher temperatures cause higher ice-cream sales.
options.feedback: A scatter plot shows association. Even a plausible causal story needs more than a plot to establish it.

options.text: There is no relationship at all, because the points flatten out at the top.
options.feedback: The flattening affects only the upper end; at lower temperatures, sales clearly rise with temperature. A changing slope is still a relationship.

options.text: The pattern looks curved, so a straight line may fit poorly at high temperatures.
options.feedback: Correct. Seeing the curve first lets you judge whether a straight line is a sensible summary.

options.text: A straight line will fit perfectly, because sales rise with temperature.
options.feedback: A straight line has the same slope everywhere, while these points rise and then level off, so a line will miss part of the pattern.

practice.explanation: Plotting first reveals the form of a relationship. A curved pattern warns that a single straight line may fit poorly in parts of the range.

practice.concept: Visual exploration before regression (Section 1.5, Key Concept 1.3)
practice.stem: Which features of a relationship can you judge by looking at a scatter plot? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Direction (positive or negative)
options.feedback: Correct: whether the points drift up or down from left to right shows the direction.

options.text: Whether X causes Y
options.feedback: A plot shows how variables move together, not cause and effect; other factors may drive both variables.

options.text: Form (straight-line or curved)
options.feedback: Correct: the overall shape of the cloud of points reveals the form.

options.text: The presence of outliers
options.feedback: Correct: unusual points stand out visually from the rest.

practice.explanation: Key Concept 1.3: scatter plots reveal direction, strength, form, and outliers. Establishing causation requires more than visual evidence.

practice.concept: Dependent and independent variables (Section 1.1, Key Concepts)
practice.stem: In the model earnings = β0 + β1 × education + ε, which is the dependent variable?

options.text: Education
options.feedback: Education is the explanatory (independent) variable: the input used to explain the outcome.

options.text: Earnings
options.feedback: Correct: earnings is the outcome being explained, so it is the dependent variable Y.

options.text: β<sub>1</sub>
options.feedback: β<sub>1</sub> is a parameter (the slope), not a variable. It describes how the outcome changes with the explanatory variable.

options.text: ε
options.feedback: ε is the error term: everything other than education that affects earnings.

practice.explanation: The dependent variable (Y) is the outcome on the left-hand side; the independent variable (X) is the explainer; β<sub>0</sub> and β<sub>1</sub> are parameters; ε is the error term.

practice.concept: Interpreting the slope (Sections 1.1, 1.6, and 1.7, Key Concept 1.4)
practice.stem: Suppose a regression gives earnings = 20,000 + 5,000 × education, where earnings are annual dollars and education is measured in years. Which statement correctly interprets 5,000?

options.text: Workers earn about $5,000 more for every additional year they have worked.
options.feedback: The X variable is years of education, not years of work experience. A slope is tied to the variable it multiplies.

options.text: Each extra year of education is associated with about $5,000 more in annual earnings.
options.feedback: Correct: the slope is the average difference in Y associated with a one-unit difference in X.

options.text: One more year of education will raise anyone's earnings by exactly $5,000.
options.feedback: Two problems: the slope describes an average association, not an exact rule for every person, and association alone does not establish what an extra year would cause.

options.text: A person with no education is predicted to earn $5,000 per year.
options.feedback: Predicted earnings at zero education is the intercept's job, and the intercept here is 20,000, not 5,000.

practice.explanation: Key Concept 1.4: the slope is the change in Y associated with a one-unit increase in X. Here, that is $5,000 of annual earnings per extra year of education, on average.

practice.concept: Interpreting the intercept (Section 1.7)
practice.stem: In earnings = 20,000 + 5,000 × education, what does 20,000 represent?

options.text: The average earnings of all workers in the sample
options.feedback: The intercept is the line's value at education = 0, which is generally different from the average earnings in the sample.

options.text: The increase in earnings for each additional year of education
options.feedback: That is the role of the slope. The intercept is where the line starts.

options.text: The predicted earnings for someone with zero years of education
options.feedback: Correct. Whether that number is meaningful depends on whether people with (nearly) zero education appear in the data.

options.text: The highest earnings anyone in the sample can have
options.feedback: A regression line is not capped at the intercept; with a positive slope, predicted earnings grow as education increases.

practice.explanation: The intercept is the predicted Y when X = 0. It is economically meaningful only when X = 0 is realistic and within (or near) the observed data.

practice.concept: Interpreting the slope: units of measurement (Key Concept 1.4)
practice.stem: A regression of monthly rent (in dollars) on apartment size (in square meters) gives a slope of 12. If rent were instead measured in thousands of dollars, what would the slope be?

options.feedback: Correct: 12 dollars is 0.012 thousand dollars, so the slope becomes 0.012 thousand dollars per square meter.
Converting dollars into thousands of dollars makes the numbers on the Y side smaller, not larger.

options.text: 12, because changing units never changes a slope
options.feedback: A slope is measured in units of Y per unit of X, so changing the units of Y changes its value (though not its meaning).
Check the conversion factor: one thousand dollars is 1,000 dollars, not 10.

practice.explanation: A slope is measured in units of Y per unit of X. Measuring Y in thousands divides every Y value, and therefore the slope, by 1,000: 12 becomes 0.012.

practice.concept: Interpreting the slope (Sections 1.1, 1.6, and 1.7, Key Concept 1.4)
practice.stem: In a simple regression, the slope coefficient tells you how much Y changes, on average, when X increases by one unit.

options.text: True
options.feedback: Correct. This is Key Concept 1.4. Remember that it describes an association, not necessarily a causal effect.

options.text: False
options.feedback: Revisit Key Concept 1.4: what does the slope measure in terms of a one-unit change in X?

practice.explanation: Key Concept 1.4: the slope measures how much Y changes when X increases by one unit. It is an association in the data.

practice.concept: Ordinary Least Squares and residuals (Sections 1.6 and 1.8)
practice.stem: Why does OLS square the residuals instead of simply adding them up?

options.text: Squaring makes the calculation faster for the computer to carry out.
options.feedback: Speed is not the reason. Think about what happens when positive and negative residuals are added together.

options.text: Positive and negative misses would cancel out; squaring makes every miss count.
options.feedback: Correct. Squared residuals are never negative, and large misses weigh more, so the criterion rewards lines that are close to all of the points.

options.text: Squaring makes all of the residuals smaller and easier to read.
options.feedback: Squaring makes residuals larger than 1 in size even bigger. Its purpose is to make all misses positive and to weigh large misses more.

options.text: Squaring turns the regression slope into a causal effect.
options.feedback: No mathematical choice in the fitting method can turn association into causation.

practice.explanation: Section 1.6: OLS minimizes the sum of squared residuals. Squaring keeps positive and negative misses from canceling out and gives extra weight to large misses.

practice.concept: Ordinary Least Squares and residuals (Sections 1.6 and 1.8)
practice.stem: Suppose predicted earnings = 20,000 + 5,000 × education. A worker with 12 years of education earns $75,000. What is this worker's residual (actual − predicted)?

options.feedback: Check the order of subtraction: residual = actual − predicted. Compare the actual earnings with the prediction carefully.
This subtracts only the intercept. The prediction must also include the slope term for 12 years of education.
That is the predicted earnings for 12 years of education, not the residual.
Correct: predicted = 20,000 + 5,000 × 12 = $80,000, so the residual is 75,000 − 80,000 = −$5,000 (the point lies below the line).

practice.explanation: Residual = actual − predicted. Predicted earnings = 20,000 + 5,000 × 12 = $80,000, so the residual is −$5,000. A negative residual means the observation lies below the fitted line.

practice.concept: Ordinary Least Squares and residuals (Sections 1.6 and 1.8)
practice.stem: A negative residual means the observation lies below the fitted line: its actual Y is smaller than its predicted Y.

options.text: True
options.feedback: Correct. Residual = actual − predicted, so a negative value means actual < predicted, which is a point below the line.

options.text: False
options.feedback: Work through the definition: residual = actual − predicted. When is that difference negative?

practice.explanation: Residuals are actual minus predicted Y: positive for points above the line, negative for points below it.

practice.concept: Reading regression output: standard error, t value, p-value (Section 1.7, Key Concept 1.5)
practice.stem: A regression reports a slope of 2.4 with a standard error of 0.8. What is the t-statistic?

options.feedback: This ratio is upside down. The t-statistic measures how many standard errors the coefficient lies away from zero.
Multiplying the coefficient by its standard error is not a meaningful statistic. The t-statistic is a ratio.
Correct: t = 2.4 ÷ 0.8 = 3.0, so the slope lies three standard errors away from zero.
Adding the coefficient and its standard error is not how the t-statistic is formed. It is a ratio.

practice.explanation: Section 1.7: t value = coefficient ÷ standard error. A larger |t| means the estimate lies further from zero relative to its uncertainty.

practice.concept: Reading regression output: standard error, t value, p-value (Section 1.7, Key Concept 1.5)
practice.stem: Two studies estimate the same slope, 50. Study A reports a standard error of 5; Study B reports a standard error of 25. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Study A's slope estimate is more precise.
options.feedback: Correct: a smaller standard error means a more precise estimate.

options.text: Study B's slope estimate is larger.
options.feedback: Both slope estimates are 50. The standard errors differ, not the estimates.

options.text: Study B's regression explains more of the variation in Y.
options.feedback: That is a question about R², which is not reported here. A standard error describes the precision of a coefficient.

options.text: The two estimates are equally precise because the slopes are equal.
options.feedback: Precision is measured by the standard error, not by the size of the estimate. Equal estimates can have very different precision.

practice.explanation: Key Concept 1.5: the standard error measures the precision of an estimate. Study A's t value is 50 ÷ 5 = 10; Study B's is 50 ÷ 25 = 2.

practice.concept: Reading regression output: standard error, t value, p-value (Section 1.7, Key Concept 1.5)
practice.stem: In regression output, which elements tell you about the statistical significance of the slope? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: The t value
options.feedback: Correct: t = coefficient ÷ standard error, and a large |t| signals significance.

options.text: The p-value, Pr(>|t|)
options.feedback: Correct: a small p-value indicates that the slope is significantly different from zero.

options.text: R²
options.feedback: R² measures the share of variation in Y that is explained. It is about fit, not about whether the slope differs significantly from zero.

options.text: The number of observations
options.feedback: The sample size affects precision, but on its own it does not tell you whether the slope is significant.

practice.explanation: Key Concept 1.5: the t-statistic and p-value address statistical significance; the standard error measures precision; R² measures fit.

practice.concept: Reading regression output: RMSE (Section 1.7)
practice.stem: A smaller RMSE means that the fitted line's predictions are, on average, further from the actual values of Y.

options.text: True
options.feedback: Revisit Section 1.7: RMSE measures the typical size of a prediction error. What does a smaller typical error mean?

options.text: False
options.feedback: Correct. RMSE is the typical size of a prediction error in the units of Y, so a smaller RMSE means predictions closer to the actual values.

practice.explanation: Section 1.7: the RMSE (root mean squared error) is the typical size of a prediction error, measured in the units of Y. A smaller RMSE means the fitted line predicts more accurately.

practice.concept: R-squared (Section 1.7, Key Concepts)
practice.stem: A regression of students' exam scores on hours studied gives R² = 0.25. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Studying causes about 25% of each student's exam score.
options.feedback: R² describes fit across the sample, not causes, and it does not split one student's score into parts.

options.text: The model predicts the scores of 25% of the students exactly.
options.feedback: R² is not a hit rate. It is the share of the overall variation captured by the line.

options.text: Each extra hour of study raises the score by 0.25 points.
options.feedback: That would be a slope. R² is a share between 0 and 1 that describes how well the line fits.

options.text: Hours studied account for about a quarter of the variation in exam scores.
options.feedback: Correct: R² is the proportion of the variation in Y explained by the regression.

practice.explanation: R² is the proportion of the variation in Y explained by X, between 0 and 1. Here hours studied explain 25% of the variation and other factors the remaining 75%. R² says nothing about causation.

practice.concept: R-squared (Section 1.7, Key Concepts)
practice.stem: Which statements about R² are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: A low R² means the slope must be zero.
options.feedback: A low R² means X explains a small share of Y's variation; X can still be clearly associated with Y.

options.text: It ranges from 0 to 1.
options.feedback: Correct: R² is a proportion of variation explained.

options.text: A high R² does not show that X causes Y.
options.feedback: Correct: R² measures fit, not causation.

options.text: It is measured in the same units as Y (for example, dollars).
options.feedback: R² is a unit-free share. The typical size of prediction errors in units of Y is reported by the RMSE.

practice.explanation: R² is a unit-free proportion between 0 and 1 that measures goodness of fit. A high R² does not imply causation, and a low R² does not mean X is irrelevant.

practice.concept: R-squared (Section 1.7, Key Concepts)
practice.stem: If a regression has R² = 0.40, then the other 60% of the variation in Y must be due to measurement errors in the data.

options.text: True
options.feedback: The unexplained part reflects everything not included in the model (other factors that affect Y), not just errors in recording the data.

options.text: False
options.feedback: Correct. The unexplained 60% comes from all factors outside the model, of which measurement error is at most one.

practice.explanation: 1 − R² is the share of variation not explained by X. It reflects omitted factors and randomness, not only measurement error. In the house model, about 38% is unexplained, which the chapter attributes to factors such as location, condition, age, and lot size.

practice.concept: Making predictions (Section 1.9)
practice.stem: Using predicted earnings = 20,000 + 5,000 × education, what are the predicted earnings of someone with 16 years of education?

options.feedback: This multiplies the slope by education but leaves out the intercept. The prediction is the whole line: intercept + slope × X.
This multiplies the intercept by education. Only the slope is multiplied by X.
This adds the slope only once. The slope must be multiplied by the number of years of education.

practice.explanation: To predict, plug X into the fitted line: 20,000 + 5,000 × 16 = $100,000.

practice.concept: Making predictions (Section 1.9)
practice.stem: Using predicted earnings = 20,000 + 5,000 × education, what is the predicted difference in earnings between someone with 16 years and someone with 12 years of education?

options.feedback: That is the difference for a single year. Scale the slope by the actual gap in years.
The intercept appears in both predictions, so it cancels when you take the difference.
Correct: 5,000 × (16 − 12) = $20,000; the intercept cancels.
This is the slope times 16 years, not times the difference in years between the two people.

practice.explanation: Predicted difference = slope × difference in X = 5,000 × 4 = $20,000. The intercept is part of both predictions, so it cancels.

practice.concept: Making predictions with the fitted line (Section 1.9, Key Concept 1.6)
practice.stem: A study of farms that used between 50 and 200 kg of fertilizer per hectare finds that each extra kg is associated with 20 kg more grain per hectare. A farmer asks what to expect from using 1,000 kg per hectare. What is the best response?

options.text: 1,000 kg is far outside the 50–200 kg range in the data, so a straight-line prediction there is unreliable.
options.feedback: Correct. This is extrapolation; the relationship may change shape outside the observed range.

options.text: Yield will rise by about 20 × 1,000 = 20,000 kg per hectare, following the estimated slope.
options.feedback: This assumes the straight-line pattern holds far beyond the data. Nothing in the data shows what happens at 1,000 kg.

options.text: The prediction is reliable as long as the regression's R² is high.
options.feedback: R² describes the fit inside the observed range. It cannot tell you whether the pattern continues far outside it.

options.text: Use the intercept, because it applies to unusually large amounts of fertilizer.
options.feedback: The intercept is the predicted yield at zero fertilizer, which is the opposite end of the scale.

practice.explanation: Key Concept 1.6: do not extrapolate beyond the range of the data. A pattern estimated between 50 and 200 kg says little about what happens at 1,000 kg.

practice.concept: Interpreting the slope: what regression can and cannot show (Section 1.9, Key Concept 1.6)
practice.stem: Across months, ice-cream sales and drowning deaths are strongly positively associated. What is the best explanation?

options.text: Eating ice cream before swimming causes people to drown.
options.feedback: The association alone cannot establish this. Is there a factor that could push both numbers up at the same time?

options.text: Hot weather raises both, so ice cream need not cause drowning.
options.feedback: Correct. Hot weather is a confounder that drives both variables, creating an association without causation.

options.text: Drownings cause people to buy more ice cream.
options.feedback: Reverse causation is worth considering, but there is no plausible mechanism here. Look for a factor that affects both variables.

options.text: The association must be a data error, because the two variables are unrelated.
options.feedback: The association is real; what is questionable is the causal interpretation, not the data.

practice.explanation: Key Concepts (Association vs. Causation): two variables can move together because a third factor drives both. Banning ice cream would not save swimmers.

practice.concept: Interpreting the slope: what regression can and cannot show (Section 1.9, Key Concept 1.6)
practice.stem: Across cities, a regression finds that cities with more police officers per capita have higher crime rates. Which explanations are possible? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: The regression proves that police cause crime.
options.feedback: A regression on observational data shows association. It cannot by itself establish which way causation runs.

options.text: Reverse causality: cities with more crime hire more police.
options.feedback: Correct: the arrow may run from crime to police rather than the other way around.

options.text: A third factor, such as city size or population density, may raise both police numbers and crime.
options.feedback: Correct: a confounder can create an association between two variables that do not cause each other.

options.text: If the R² were high enough, we could be sure that police cause crime.
options.feedback: R² measures fit, not causation. A very tight association can still be driven by reverse causality or confounders.

practice.explanation: An association can arise from causation in either direction or from omitted (confounding) variables that drive both. Regression alone cannot tell these apart.

practice.concept: Caveats when applying regression results (Section 1.9)
practice.stem: A regression using data on U.S. workers in 1990 finds that each extra year of education is associated with $5,000 higher annual earnings. A policymaker wants to apply this number to workers in Kenya in 2026. What is the most appropriate caution?

options.text: The number must first be converted into Kenyan shillings; after that, it applies directly.
options.feedback: Converting the currency changes the units but not the underlying issue: the estimate describes one labor market at one time.

options.text: The estimate is useless everywhere, including for U.S. workers in 1990.
options.feedback: Within its own setting, the estimate is a valid summary of the association. The question is whether it carries over to a different setting.

options.text: There is no issue, because education is valuable in every country.
options.feedback: Even if education is valuable everywhere, the size of the association can differ greatly across countries and decades.

options.text: Results are sample-specific: the relationship may differ in another country and time period.
options.feedback: Correct. Labor markets, education systems, and prices differ across places and decades, so the association may not carry over.

practice.explanation: Section 1.9: results are sample-specific. An estimate from one place and time may not generalize to other locations, time periods, or populations.

exam.concept: Descriptive analysis vs. statistical inference (Section 1.1, Key Concept 1.1)
exam.stem: Researcher 1 uses the 29 Davis house sales to report that the average sale price in the sample was $253,910, and stops there. Researcher 2 uses the same 29 sales to draw conclusions about how size relates to price for Davis houses in general. How are the two analyses best described?

options.text: Both are statistical inference, because any number computed from data is an inference.
options.feedback: Not every number computed from data is an inference. What makes an analysis inferential is whether it draws conclusions beyond the observed sample; apply that test to each researcher separately.

options.text: Both are descriptive analysis, because both use the same 29 houses.
options.feedback: Using the same data does not settle the question. What matters is the goal of each analysis (Key Concept 1.1).

options.text: Researcher 1 does statistical inference; Researcher 2 does descriptive analysis.
options.feedback: Revisit Key Concept 1.1 and apply each definition to what each researcher actually claims.

options.text: Researcher 1 does descriptive analysis; Researcher 2 does statistical inference.
options.feedback: Correct. Summarizing the sample in hand is descriptive analysis; using the sample to learn about the wider population of houses is statistical inference.

exam.explanation: Key Concept 1.1: descriptive analysis summarizes the data you have (averages, tables, plots); statistical inference uses a sample to draw conclusions about a broader population. Researcher 1 describes; Researcher 2 generalizes, which is inference. Most econometric analysis is inference.

exam.concept: Observational vs. experimental data (Section 1.4, Key Concept 1.2)
exam.stem: The Davis data record the sizes and prices of houses that happened to sell in 1999; nobody assigned sizes to houses. Why does this matter when interpreting the regression of price on size?

options.text: Houses of different sizes may also differ in other ways, which makes causal conclusions harder.
options.feedback: Correct. In observational data, size comes bundled with other house characteristics, so the regression cannot by itself separate the effect of size from the effects of those other differences.

options.text: It does not matter: with 29 houses, observational and experimental data lead to the same conclusions.
options.feedback: Sample size does not erase the difference. What distinguishes experimental from observational data is whether the conditions were controlled, not how many observations there are.

options.text: Observational data cannot be used for regression analysis, so the estimates are invalid.
options.feedback: Observational data are the everyday raw material of econometrics, and regression is routinely applied to them.

options.text: Observational data are always measured less accurately than experimental data, so the slope is imprecise.
options.feedback: Measurement accuracy is a separate issue. Observational data can be measured very precisely; the challenge is that the conditions were not controlled by the researcher.

exam.explanation: Key Concept 1.2: economics relies mainly on observational data, meaning behavior observed in uncontrolled settings. Without control over who gets which conditions, other factors can move together with X, so establishing causal effects requires careful methods.

exam.concept: Observational vs. experimental data (Section 1.4, Key Concept 1.2)
exam.stem: Economics relies mainly on experimental data, because economists can usually assign conditions such as income or education at random.

options.text: True
options.feedback: Think about where economic data usually come from: records of choices that people, firms, and governments already made. Randomly assigning incomes or years of education is rarely feasible or ethical.

options.text: False
options.feedback: Correct. Economics relies mainly on observational data. Experiments exist, but most economic data come from observing behavior in uncontrolled settings.

exam.explanation: Most economic data are observational (Key Concept 1.2). That is why causal questions in economics need careful methods: the researcher did not control who received which conditions.

exam.concept: Types of variables: continuous, discrete, categorical (Key Takeaways)
exam.stem: Which of the following are discrete numerical variables? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Annual rainfall in a city, in millimeters
options.feedback: Rainfall can take any value within a range (812.4 mm, 812.45 mm, …), which makes it continuous rather than discrete.

options.text: Number of bedrooms in a house
options.feedback: Correct: bedrooms are counted in whole numbers (3, 4, 5, …), so the variable is discrete numerical.

options.text: Number of employees at a firm
options.feedback: Correct: employees are counted in whole numbers, so this is discrete numerical.

options.text: The world region where a country is located (Africa, Asia, Europe, …)
options.feedback: Region names are labels for groups, not numbers you can count or measure. That makes this variable categorical.

options.text: Number of cars a household owns
options.feedback: Correct: cars are counted in whole numbers, so this is discrete numerical.

exam.explanation: Discrete numerical variables take countable values (often whole numbers); continuous variables can take any value in a range; categorical variables place observations into groups. Bedrooms and employees are counts, so they are discrete.

exam.concept: Data structures: cross-section, time series, panel (Key Takeaways)
exam.stem: A survey follows the same 500 households every year from 2015 to 2024, recording each household's income. What kind of data are these?

options.text: Panel data
options.feedback: Correct: the same units (households) are observed repeatedly over time, which is the defining feature of panel data.

options.text: Cross-section data
options.feedback: Cross-section data observe many units at a single point in time. Here each household appears in ten different years.

options.text: Time-series data
options.feedback: Time-series data follow a single unit over time. Count the units in this survey.

options.text: Experimental data
options.feedback: Nothing was assigned or controlled by the researcher; the survey simply records income. The question is about how the data are organized across units and time.

exam.explanation: Cross-section: many units at one time. Time series: one unit over time. Panel: many units, each observed over time; here, 500 households × 10 years.

exam.concept: Data structures: cross-section, time series, panel (Key Takeaways)
exam.stem: The Davis house dataset (29 different houses, each sold once in 1999) is an example of panel data.

options.text: True
options.feedback: Panel data require the same units to be observed at several points in time. Each Davis house appears only once, at one point in time.

options.text: False
options.feedback: Correct. Many different units observed at a single point in time form a cross-section, the type of data this book focuses on.

exam.explanation: The house dataset is a cross-section: 29 units (houses) observed once, in 1999. Panel data would follow the same houses over several years.

exam.concept: Visual exploration before regression (Section 1.5, Key Concept 1.3)
exam.stem: Why does Chapter 1 recommend plotting price against size before running the regression?

options.text: Because OLS cannot be computed by the software until a scatter plot has been drawn.
options.feedback: OLS is a calculation on the numbers; software will compute it without any plot. The reason to plot first is about what you, the analyst, learn.

options.text: Because it shows the direction, form, and strength of the relationship, plus outliers.
options.feedback: Correct. Plotting first shows whether a straight line is a sensible summary and flags unusual points before they shape your conclusions.

options.text: Because a scatter plot shows whether house size causes higher prices.
options.feedback: No plot can establish causation by itself. A scatter plot shows how two variables move together, which is association.

options.text: Because the scatter plot shows the exact value of the slope before any calculation.
options.feedback: A scatter plot gives an impression of the direction and steepness of a pattern, but the slope's value comes from the OLS calculation.

exam.explanation: Key Concept 1.3: always plot first. A scatter plot reveals direction (positive or negative), form (linear or curved), strength, and outliers, which a table of summary statistics can hide.

exam.concept: Visual exploration before regression (Section 1.5, Key Concept 1.3)
exam.stem: In the scatter plot of price (vertical axis) against size (horizontal axis) for the 29 houses, the points drift upward from left to right and roughly follow a straight-line pattern, but they do not lie exactly on a line. Which conclusions does this support? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Larger houses tend to sell for higher prices (a positive relationship).
options.feedback: Correct: an upward drift from left to right signals a positive association.

options.text: Size fully determines price.
options.feedback: If size fully determined price, every point would sit exactly on the pattern. The spread of points around it says otherwise.

options.text: Size and price are unrelated, because the points do not lie exactly on a line.
options.feedback: Points can scatter around a pattern and still show a clear relationship. Revisit Section 1.5.

options.text: A straight line is a reasonable first summary of the pattern.
options.feedback: Correct: the points roughly follow a straight-line pattern, so a linear regression is a sensible starting point.

exam.explanation: Section 1.5 reads the plot for direction (positive), form (roughly linear), and scatter (points off the line, which is the variation that size cannot explain). None of these is a causal statement.

exam.concept: Visual exploration before regression (Section 1.5, Key Concept 1.3)
exam.stem: Two datasets have identical means and standard deviations for X and for Y. In the first, the scatter plot shows points rising along a straight line; in the second, the points form a U shape. What does this illustrate?

options.text: The two datasets must be identical, since their summary statistics match.
options.feedback: Ask what means and standard deviations record about each variable, and what they leave out.

options.text: Summary statistics can hide the form of a relationship; a plot reveals it.
options.feedback: Correct. Means and standard deviations describe each variable separately; a plot reveals how the two move together, and in what shape.

options.text: A straight regression line will summarize both datasets equally well.
options.feedback: A straight line can summarize a straight-line pattern well, but it cannot follow a U shape: it would miss the curve entirely.

options.text: One of the two scatter plots must have been drawn incorrectly.
options.feedback: Nothing in the description suggests a plotting mistake. Ask what means and standard deviations do and do not record.

exam.explanation: Key Concept 1.3: summary statistics alone can miss nonlinearities and outliers. Plotting first shows the form of the relationship and whether a straight line is a sensible model.

exam.concept: The regression model and the error term (Section 1.1)
exam.stem: In the model price = β<sub>0</sub> + β<sub>1</sub> × size + ε, what does the error term ε represent?

options.text: The difference between the intercept β<sub>0</sub> and the slope β<sub>1</sub>.
options.feedback: β<sub>0</sub> and β<sub>1</sub> are the two parameters of the line; ε is a separate part of the model that varies from house to house.

options.text: A mistake made when the prices and sizes were recorded in the dataset.
options.feedback: Recording mistakes, if any, would be only a small part of ε; even perfectly recorded data would still have an error term. Revisit how Section 1.1 describes ε.

options.text: Everything other than size that affects price.
options.feedback: Correct. ε collects all the other influences on price (location, condition, bargaining, …) that size does not capture.

options.text: The predicted price of a house of a given size.
options.feedback: The predicted price is the value on the fitted line, β<sub>0</sub> + β<sub>1</sub> × size. ε is a separate term in the model; revisit Section 1.1.

exam.explanation: Section 1.1: ε is the error term, the random variation in price not explained by size. In the estimated model, the residuals (actual minus predicted price) play this role.

exam.concept: Interpreting the slope (Sections 1.1, 1.6, and 1.7, Key Concept 1.4)
exam.stem: The fitted line is predicted price = 115,017 + 73.77 × size. Which statement correctly interprets the number 73.77?

options.text: Each house in the sample sold for $73.77 per square foot.
options.feedback: $73.77 is not what each house sold for per square foot: average price divided by average size is about $135 per square foot here. Revisit what the slope measures (Key Concept 1.4).

options.text: Adding one square foot to a house will raise its sale price by $73.77.
options.feedback: This describes what would happen if one particular house were enlarged. Revisit what a regression on observational data can show (Key Concept 1.6).

options.text: Houses that are one square foot larger tend to sell for about $73.77 more.
options.feedback: Correct. The slope is the average difference in price associated with a one-square-foot difference in size: an association, not a guaranteed effect.

options.text: A house of 73.77 square feet would be predicted to sell for $115,017.
options.feedback: This mixes up the roles of the numbers: 115,017 is the predicted price when size is zero, and 73.77 is a rate of change, not a size.

exam.explanation: Key Concept 1.4: the slope is the change in Y associated with a one-unit increase in X. Here that is about $73.77 more in price for each additional square foot, on average across houses.

exam.concept: Interpreting the intercept (Section 1.7)
exam.stem: Is the intercept of $115,017 economically meaningful in the house-price regression?

options.text: Yes: it estimates the value of an empty lot (land with no house) in Davis.
options.feedback: Nothing in this regression measures land values: it uses only the sizes and sale prices of houses that sold. Revisit what the intercept represents (Section 1.7).

options.text: Yes: it equals the average sale price of the 29 houses in the sample.
options.feedback: The average sale price in the sample is about $253,910, not $115,017. Revisit what the intercept represents (Section 1.7).

options.text: No: its p-value shows that it is not statistically significant.
options.feedback: Check the premise: the intercept's t value is above 5, so a lack of statistical significance cannot be the reason.

options.text: No: 0 sq ft lies far outside the observed 1,400–3,300 sq ft range.
options.feedback: Correct. No house has zero square feet, so the intercept is best seen as the anchor that positions the line, not as a price anyone would pay.

exam.explanation: Section 1.7: the intercept is the predicted Y when X = 0. Here X = 0 means a house with no floor space, far outside the data, so the intercept is not economically meaningful on its own; the slope is the number of interest.

exam.concept: Interpreting the slope: units of measurement (Key Concept 1.4, Section 1.9)
exam.stem: Suppose house size were recorded in hundreds of square feet instead of square feet (so a 1,900 sq ft house has size = 19), with price still in dollars. What would the estimated slope become?

options.text: About $0.74 per hundred square feet
options.feedback: Think about what a one-unit change in the new size variable means for a house, and whether a bigger change in size should go with a bigger or smaller change in price.

options.text: About $7,377 per hundred square feet
options.feedback: Correct. One unit now means 100 sq ft, so the slope scales up by 100: 73.77 × 100 ≈ $7,377.

options.text: Still $73.77, because the regression describes the same relationship
options.feedback: The fit does not change (R² stays the same), but revisit what the slope measures: a change in Y per one unit of X.

options.text: About $737.70 per hundred square feet
options.feedback: Check the scaling factor you applied against the way the new size variable is defined in the question.

exam.explanation: The slope measures the change in Y per one-unit change in X. If one unit of X becomes 100 times larger, the slope becomes 100 times larger: 73.77 × 100 ≈ $7,377 per 100 sq ft, consistent with Section 1.9's '100 sq ft larger ≈ $7,400 more'.

exam.concept: Dependent and independent variables (Section 1.1, Key Concepts)
exam.stem: Treating price as Y and size as X is a modeling decision; a regression of size on price would answer a different question.

options.text: True
options.feedback: Correct. Regressing price on size asks how price differs with size; regressing size on price asks how size differs with price, which is a different question with a different slope.

options.text: False
options.feedback: Swapping Y and X changes the question being asked. The roles are chosen by the analyst to match the question, not dictated by the data.

exam.explanation: Key Concepts (Y and X): the dependent variable Y is the outcome to explain; the independent variable X is the explainer. Choosing which is which is a modeling decision tied to the question you want to answer.

exam.concept: Ordinary Least Squares and residuals (Sections 1.6 and 1.8)
exam.stem: Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) chooses the intercept and slope that minimize which quantity?

options.text: The sum of the residuals (actual minus predicted Y)
options.feedback: Residuals can be positive or negative, so they can cancel out; many poor lines would make their simple sum close to zero. OLS needs a criterion that counts every miss.

options.text: The number of points that do not lie exactly on the line
options.feedback: OLS cares about how far points are from the line, not just whether they are on it. A line through two points that misses the rest badly would do well on this count.

options.text: The sum of the squared residuals (squared vertical distances)
options.feedback: Correct. Squaring makes every miss positive and penalizes large misses more heavily.

options.text: The sum of the squared horizontal distances to the line
options.feedback: Revisit Section 1.8: how is a residual defined, and which variable's prediction error does it measure?

exam.explanation: Section 1.6: OLS chooses β<sub>0</sub> and β<sub>1</sub> to minimize Σ(price<sub>i</sub> − β<sub>0</sub> − β<sub>1</sub> × size<sub>i</sub>)². A residual is the vertical gap between a point and the line.

exam.concept: Ordinary Least Squares and residuals (Sections 1.6 and 1.8)
exam.stem: Suppose a 2,000 sq ft house sold for $270,000. Using predicted price = 115,017 + 73.77 × size, what is its residual (actual price − predicted price)?

options.text: About +$7,443: it sold for more than the line predicts.
About −$7,443: it sold for less than the line predicts.
options.feedback: Check the order of subtraction in the definition of a residual (Section 1.8).

options.text: About $154,983, the price left after removing the intercept.
options.feedback: The amount subtracted here is not this house's predicted price. Revisit how a prediction is formed from the fitted line (Section 1.9).

options.text: About $262,557, the price the fitted line assigns to it.
options.feedback: This is a value on the fitted line, not a residual. Revisit how Section 1.8 defines a residual.

exam.explanation: A residual is actual Y minus predicted Y. The predicted price for 2,000 sq ft is 115,017 + 73.77 × 2,000 = $262,557, so the residual is 270,000 − 262,557 = +$7,443. Points with positive residuals sit above the line.

exam.concept: Ordinary Least Squares and residuals (Sections 1.6 and 1.8)
exam.stem: Which statements about OLS residuals in the house-price regression are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: OLS chooses the line so that every residual equals zero.
options.feedback: With 29 scattered houses, no straight line can pass through every point. OLS makes the residuals as small as possible overall, not zero.

options.text: A positive residual means the house sold for less than the line predicts.
options.feedback: Check the sign convention: residual = actual − predicted. What must be true of the actual price for that difference to be positive?

options.text: A residual is the vertical gap between a house's actual price and the price predicted by the line.
options.feedback: Correct: residual = actual price − predicted price, the vertical distance from the point to the line.

options.text: Houses far from the line have more influence on where OLS places it than houses slightly off it.
options.feedback: Correct: squaring makes a residual twice as big count four times as much, so large misses pull hard on the fitted line.

options.text: Residuals are measured in square feet, the units of house size.
options.feedback: Revisit which variable's prediction error a residual measures, and in which units (Section 1.8).

exam.explanation: Residuals are vertical gaps (actual − predicted). OLS minimizes their sum of squares, so large misses carry extra weight. Positive residuals lie above the line, negative ones below it.

exam.concept: Reading regression output: standard error, t value, p-value (Section 1.7, Key Concept 1.5)
exam.stem: The output reports a size coefficient of 73.771 with a standard error of 11.175. What is the t-statistic, and what does it tell you?

options.text: About 0.15: the coefficient is small relative to its standard error.
options.feedback: Check how the t value is formed from the coefficient and its standard error (Section 1.7).

options.text: About 824: the coefficient is very large relative to its standard error.
options.feedback: Multiplying the coefficient by its standard error does not give the t value. Revisit how Section 1.7 defines it.

options.text: About 6.60: there is a 6.60% chance that size and price are unrelated.
options.feedback: A t-statistic is not a probability. Revisit what Section 1.7 says the t value and the p-value each report.

options.text: About 6.60: the estimate lies more than six standard errors away from zero.
options.feedback: Correct. t = 73.771 ÷ 11.175 ≈ 6.60. An estimate this many standard errors from zero is strong evidence that the slope is not zero.

exam.explanation: Section 1.7: t value = coefficient ÷ standard error = 73.771 ÷ 11.175 ≈ 6.60. The slope is more than six standard errors from zero. The p-value (below 0.001) adds the probability statement: a pattern this strong would be very unlikely if size and price were unrelated in the population.

exam.concept: Reading regression output: standard error, t value, p-value (Section 1.7, Key Concept 1.5)
exam.stem: Which statements about the elements of the regression output are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: The standard error measures how precisely the slope is estimated; smaller means more precise.
options.feedback: Correct: the standard error describes the precision of the estimate.

options.text: The p-value helps judge whether the slope differs significantly from zero.
options.feedback: Correct: a small p-value indicates that the slope is significantly different from zero.

options.text: R² tells you whether the slope is statistically significant.
options.feedback: R² measures how much of the variation in Y the regression accounts for. Statistical significance is judged from other parts of the output.

options.text: The intercept is the main result of interest in this regression.
options.feedback: In the house regression, the intercept mainly anchors the line (a 0 sq ft house is not meaningful). The question of interest is how price varies with size.

exam.explanation: Key Concept 1.5: the coefficient gives the size and direction of the relationship; the standard error gives its precision; the t value and p-value address statistical significance; R² gives the share of variation explained.

exam.concept: Reading regression output: standard error, t value, p-value (Section 1.7, Key Concept 1.5)
exam.stem: The size coefficient has a p-value below 0.001. This means that, if size and price were truly unrelated in the population, a sample relationship at least as strong as the one estimated would be very unlikely.

options.text: True
options.feedback: Correct. A tiny p-value says the data would be very surprising if there were no relationship in the population, which is strong evidence that the slope is not zero.

options.text: False
options.feedback: Revisit Section 1.7's reading of 'p < 0.001': a p-value describes how surprising the estimate would be if size and price were unrelated in the population.

exam.explanation: A small p-value signals statistical significance: an estimate at least this far from zero would be very unlikely if the true slope were zero. It does not, by itself, say that the relationship is causal or economically large. Chapters 3, 4, and 7 develop these tools.

exam.concept: Reading regression output: RMSE (Section 1.7)
exam.stem: The house-price regression reports an RMSE of 22,724. This means that a typical gap between a house's actual sale price and its predicted price is roughly $22,700.

options.text: True
options.feedback: Correct. The RMSE (root mean squared error) is the typical size of a prediction error, measured in the units of Y, which is dollars here.

options.text: False
options.feedback: Revisit Section 1.7: in what units is the RMSE measured, and what kind of error does it summarize?

exam.explanation: Section 1.7: the RMSE is the typical size of a prediction error, in the units of Y. For the house model, actual prices typically differ from the fitted line by roughly $22,700. A smaller RMSE means more accurate predictions.

exam.concept: R-squared (Section 1.7, Key Concepts)
exam.stem: The house-price regression has R² = 0.6175. Which statement is correct?

options.text: House size causes about 62% of each house's sale price.
options.feedback: R² says nothing about causes, and it does not split a single house's price into parts.

options.text: Size accounts for about 62% of the variation in sale prices in the sample.
options.feedback: Correct. R² is the proportion of the variation in Y that the regression explains.

options.text: Predicted prices are typically off by about 38% of a house's actual price.
options.feedback: R² is not a percentage error for each house. Revisit what R² measures (Section 1.7).

options.text: Each additional square foot raises the sale price by about 0.6175%.
options.feedback: That would be a slope, not R². R² is a share between 0 and 1 that summarizes fit, not a rate of change.

exam.explanation: R² = 0.6175: size accounts for about 62% of the variation in prices in this sample; the remaining 38% or so reflects other factors. A high R² does not imply causation.

exam.concept: R-squared (Section 1.7, Key Concepts)
exam.stem: Using the same 29 houses, a regression of price on the number of bedrooms gives R² ≈ 0.18, while the regression of price on size gives R² ≈ 0.62. What can you conclude?

options.text: In this sample, size accounts for far more of the variation in prices than bedrooms do.
options.feedback: Correct. Comparing R² across simple regressions with the same Y shows which single variable tracks Y more closely in this sample.

options.text: The number of bedrooms has no association at all with sale price in this sample.
options.feedback: An R² of 0.18 is not zero. What does a nonzero R² say about whether two variables move together?

options.text: Size has a larger causal effect on sale price than the number of bedrooms has.
options.feedback: R² measures fit, not causation. A higher R² does not tell you which variable would change price more if you intervened.

options.text: One regression must contain an error, since R² should be similar for any predictor of the same Y.
options.feedback: Different predictors can track Y very differently. There is no reason for R² to be similar across them.

exam.explanation: R² shows how much of the variation in price each single predictor accounts for: about 62% for size versus about 18% for bedrooms. Neither number speaks to causation.

exam.concept: R-squared (Section 1.7, Key Concepts)
exam.stem: With real-world economic data, an R² well below 1 means that the regression is useless and should be discarded.

options.text: True
options.feedback: Economic outcomes depend on many factors that no single regression includes. Would that make the house model, with R² = 0.6175, useless?

options.text: False
options.feedback: Correct. With economic data, R² values well below 1 are normal, because many unmeasured factors affect outcomes. A modest R² does not make an estimated slope useless.

exam.explanation: R² ranges from 0 to 1. With economic data, many unmeasured factors influence outcomes, so an R² well below 1 is normal. The house model's R² of 0.6175 leaves about 38% of the variation unexplained, yet the slope is still precisely estimated and informative.

exam.concept: Making predictions (Section 1.9)
exam.stem: Using predicted price = 115,017 + 73.77 × size, what is the predicted price of a 2,500 sq ft house?

options.feedback: This is not the full predicted price. Revisit how a prediction is formed from the fitted line (Section 1.9).
That is the average sale price in the sample, which ignores this house's size. Revisit how a prediction is formed (Section 1.9).
Check how size enters the prediction formula (Section 1.9).

exam.explanation: Plug X into the fitted line: 115,017 + 73.77 × 2,500 = $299,442. Because 2,500 sq ft lies inside the observed range (1,400–3,300 sq ft), this prediction does not extrapolate.

exam.concept: Making predictions (Section 1.9)
exam.stem: Two houses in the sample differ in size by 300 sq ft. Using the fitted line, by how much do their predicted prices differ?

options.text: About $7,400
options.feedback: This figure corresponds to a different size gap from the one in the question.

options.text: About $22,131
options.feedback: Correct: the intercept cancels out when you compare two houses, so the difference is 73.77 × 300 ≈ $22,131.
Check which parts of the two predictions differ between the houses and which are the same.

options.text: It depends on how large the two houses are.
options.feedback: A straight line has the same slope at every size, so where the two houses sit along the line does not matter.

exam.explanation: Predicted difference = slope × difference in X = 73.77 × 300 ≈ $22,131. On a straight line the intercept cancels, and the same 300 sq ft gap implies the same predicted difference anywhere along the line.

exam.concept: Making predictions with the fitted line (Section 1.9, Key Concept 1.6)
exam.stem: A developer asks you to use the fitted line to predict the price of a 6,000 sq ft house in Davis. What is the best response?

options.text: The prediction (about $557,600) is reliable, because the line extends to any size.
options.feedback: Revisit the caveats in Section 1.9 about using the fitted line for prediction.

options.text: The prediction (about $557,600) is reliable, because R² is above 0.5.
options.feedback: R² summarizes how well the line fits the houses in the sample. Revisit the caveats in Section 1.9.

options.text: Decline: a fitted line can describe only the 29 houses already sold, not predict new ones.
options.feedback: Predicting for houses outside the sample is a standard use of a fitted line; Section 1.9 does it for a 2,000 sq ft house. Ask what is different about this request.

options.text: The line gives about $557,600, but that size is far beyond the houses in the data.
options.feedback: Correct. This is extrapolation: the data cover only 1,400–3,300 sq ft, and the relationship may not stay linear far beyond the observed sizes, so the prediction is unreliable.

exam.explanation: Key Concept 1.6: do not extrapolate. The data cover 1,400–3,300 sq ft, so a prediction at 6,000 sq ft (115,017 + 73.77 × 6,000 ≈ $557,600) relies on an assumption the data cannot check.

exam.concept: Interpreting the slope: what regression can and cannot show (Section 1.9, Key Concept 1.6)
exam.stem: A homeowner plans to add a 100 sq ft room, expecting the sale price to rise by about $7,400 because of the estimated slope. What is the main problem with this reasoning?

options.text: The slope compares different houses; it is not the effect of enlarging one.
options.feedback: Correct. The slope compares houses that differ in size, and possibly in other features that travel with size; it does not tell you what enlarging one particular house would do.

options.text: The arithmetic is wrong: 100 × 73.77 is only about $737.
options.feedback: Check the arithmetic: 100 × 73.77 = 7,377, close to $7,400. The problem lies elsewhere.

options.text: The slope applies only to houses of exactly the average size (about 1,883 sq ft).
options.feedback: A straight-line slope is the same at every point on the line. Where the house sits in the size range is not the issue here.

options.text: There is no problem, because the slope is statistically significant (p < 0.001).
options.feedback: Revisit what statistical significance does and does not establish (Key Concepts 1.5 and 1.6).

exam.explanation: Key Concept 1.6 and the chapter's Key Concepts: regression measures association. Size is correlated with other house features, so the slope mixes the effect of size with the effects of those features. What adding a room to one house would do is a causal question that the regression alone cannot answer.

exam.concept: Interpreting the slope: what regression can and cannot show (Section 1.9, Key Concept 1.6)
exam.stem: Which of the following could be omitted variables, related to both house size and price, that make the $73.77 slope a poor guide to the causal effect of size? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Quality of construction
options.feedback: Correct: better-built houses may be larger and also command higher prices.

options.text: Neighborhood or location
options.feedback: Correct: some neighborhoods have both larger houses and higher prices for reasons beyond size.

options.text: The software used to estimate the regression (Python or Stata)
options.feedback: Software does not change the data or the estimates; any correct OLS routine gives the same slope. An omitted variable must be a feature of the houses that relates to both size and price.

options.text: Condition of the house (maintenance and renovations)
options.feedback: Correct: well-kept or renovated houses may be larger (because of additions) and also sell for more.

options.text: A random number assigned to each house by a computer
options.feedback: A randomly generated number is, by construction, unrelated to both size and price, so it cannot distort the slope.

exam.explanation: An omitted variable distorts the slope when it is related to both X and Y. Construction quality, location, and condition plausibly move with size and also affect price, so the regression may attribute their influence to size.

exam.concept: Caveats when applying regression results (Section 1.9)
exam.stem: A real-estate agent in Tokyo in 2026 wants to price apartments using the estimate of $73.77 per square foot. What is the main concern?

options.text: The estimate applies directly once it is adjusted for inflation between 1999 and 2026.
options.feedback: Adjusting for inflation changes the number but cannot by itself make the estimate applicable. Revisit the caveats in Section 1.9.

options.text: The estimate is wrong, because the regression has an R² below 1.
options.feedback: An R² below 1 is normal with economic data and does not by itself make an estimate wrong. Revisit the caveats in Section 1.9.

options.text: Davis in 1999 may differ from Tokyo in 2026, so the relationship may not carry over.
options.feedback: Correct. Results are sample-specific: a different city, housing type, and decade can have a very different price–size relationship.

options.text: With only 29 houses, the slope is too imprecise to be useful even in Davis.
